title: Insufficient funds (HTTP 402) returned during deepseek/deepseek-r1 call in Next.js
symptoms: API request fails with HTTP Status Code 402
Console error: 'insufficient_funds: User does not have enough credits to complete this operation'
The promise rejected with an error object containing the code 'insufficient_funds'
root_cause: The client-side User-Pays model requires the end-user to have microcents in their Puter account to invoke AI models. This error triggers when the active user (either logged-in or temporary guest) exhausts their credit allotment or has a zero balance.

title: Temporary guest user token exhaustion in Vue on MS Edge
symptoms: Unregistered guest session suddenly fails when calling puter.auth.signIn()
Network console shows 402 Payment Required
App works initially, but fails after a few high-token generation requests
root_cause: Puter.js automatically generates a temporary guest user account if the user isn't logged in. These temporary accounts are seeded with a small amount of free credit (microcents) for onboarding. High-token models like meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct exhaust this free quota very rapidly, resulting in an HTTP 402 code.

title: Microcents allocation calculation mismatch for streaming requests in Nuxt.js
symptoms: Streaming session cuts off midway through completion
The async iterable throws an error: 'insufficient_funds' during chunk retrieval
Credits are deducted but the response remains incomplete
root_cause: When streaming AI responses with Puter.js, credits are consumed dynamically per token chunk. If the user's microcents balance drops below the required minimum mid-stream, Puter's gateway terminates the connection, throwing an out-of-funds error.

title: Monthly usage rate limiting vs credit exhaustion error in Angular with Node.js VM
symptoms: Unclear console messages mixing up rate limits (429) and out of credit error (402)
Puter API calls fail even though billing account is active
Network responses return puter.net.fetch() failures with status 402
root_cause: Puter.js accounts have a safety daily/monthly microcents ceiling (limit) configured in their dashboard settings to prevent accidental runaway loops or billing shocks. Once reached, Puter APIs return insufficient funds (402) or rate limits (429) depending on threshold configurations.
solution:
1. Use `puter.auth.getDetailedAppUsage()` to inspect exact API consumption metrics.
2. Adjust the daily safety limits inside the Puter Developer Dashboard.
3. Ensure your loop bounds are correctly structured to avoid infinite generation loops that drain user microcents in seconds.

title: Authentication popup blocked on Chrome when initiating signIn in Svelte
symptoms: Call to `puter.auth.signIn()` resolving to nothing or rejecting silently
Web browser warning banner: 'Popup blocked'
Users report clicking the login button does nothing
root_cause: Modern web browsers block popups that are not triggered by direct, synchronous user interactions (like a `click` or `keypress` event handler). If `puter.auth.signIn()` is called inside an asynchronous callback (such as after an `await` fetch statement or inside a timeout/promise chain), the browser marks it as automated and blocks the window.

title: Ad-blockers and privacy settings block guest user frame creation in Firefox
symptoms: Puter.js fails to initialize on page load
Browser console shows blocked frame: 'iframe src: auth.puter.com/guest'
Console error: 'Failed to access localStorage/cookies inside iframe'
root_cause: To maintain guest user sessions without requiring sign-in, Puter.js embeds a silent iframe targeting `auth.puter.com` to share state. Strict privacy settings, Brave Shield, or ad-blocking extensions (like uBlock Origin) might classify this third-party iframe as a tracking mechanism and block its creation or disable its access to storage.

title: Auth popup fails to return session token to Astro in Safari Private Mode
symptoms: Authentication popup opens and signs in successfully, but original window never receives login event
Popup window remains open or closes without logging the user in
Original window reports 'isSignedIn() => false' indefinitely
root_cause: In Private/Incognito tabs or under strict cross-origin policies, browsers block the communication between the popup window (`auth.puter.com`) and the opener window (`window.opener.postMessage`). This blocks Puter's JS SDK from receiving the callback event containing the credentials.
solution:
1. Ensure that the parent page and popup have appropriate communication permissions. Avoid hosting Puter apps inside deeply nested double-iframes.
2. Advise the user to turn off strict cross-site tracking prevention or private browsing tabs if they experience infinite authorization loops.
3. Make sure you don't override the `window.name` or clear `window.opener` inside custom scripts.

title: Puter.js fails to initialize with secure context error on non-local domain
symptoms: Console warning: 'Puter.js requires a secure context (HTTPS) to function correctly.'
Auth and Storage functions throw exceptions or fail silently
Network requests to Puter API fail on non-HTTPS staging sites
root_cause: Puter.js relies heavily on modern Web Cryptography API and service workers for secure token storage and background syncing. Browser security specifications explicitly restrict these APIs to 'Secure Contexts' (HTTPS websites and `http://localhost` or `http://127.0.0.1`). Any deployment to HTTP custom domains or IP addresses will block these APIs, causing Puter.js to fail.
solution:
1. Deploy your web application with SSL enabled. Most providers like Vercel, Netlify, or Puter Hosting provide free automatic SSL certificates.
2. If self-hosting, configure a reverse proxy (like Nginx, Caddy) to terminate SSL and serve your site via HTTPS.
3. For local development on custom subdomains or IP addresses (e.g. `192.168.1.5:3000`), use tools like `mkcert` to generate local SSL certificates, or forward port traffic using SSH tunneling.

title: Localhost IP binding (e.g., http://192.168.x.x) blocking Puter.js on mobile browser testing
symptoms: App works perfectly on desktop `http://localhost:5173`
App fails to run when testing on mobile phone connected to `http://192.168.1.50:5173`
Mobile browser debug log reports that cryptographic APIs are undefined
root_cause: Browsers treat `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` as special safe secure contexts over HTTP. However, when you access your development server via its LAN IP address (`192.168.x.x`), the browser does NOT classify it as a secure context, blocking crucial Web Crypto APIs that Puter.js needs.
solution:
1. Serve the local dev site over HTTPS during LAN mobile tests. Many modern bundlers support this (e.g., `vite --https`).
2. Use a tunnel service like Ngrok, LocalTunnel, or Cloudflare Tunnels to get a free, secure public HTTPS URL pointing to your local server.
3. In Chrome, you can override secure context requirements for testing: Navigate to `chrome://flags/#unsafely-treat-insecure-origin-as-secure`, add `http://192.168.x.x:port` to the list, enable it, and relaunch Chrome.

title: Node.js Serverless Worker sandbox error: undefined globals inside serverless context
symptoms: Dynamic code evaluation throws: 'ReferenceError: fetch is not defined' or 'window is not defined'
Serverless worker crashes when using standard APIs inside Node VM
Puter workers fail when executing third-party scripts that expect a complete Node/Web environment
root_cause: Puter serverless workers run backend code inside sandboxed execution rums utilizing V8 virtual machine modules (similar to Node's `vm.runInNewContext`). This isolated environment strips dangerous native globals (like direct file system access, process controls, or global network bindings) to secure the host infrastructure. If your script relies on un-sandboxed globals or expects Node core modules, it will crash.
solution:
1. Use Puter's explicit standard libraries provided within the VM context (e.g., use Puter's built-in file APIs instead of native Node `fs`).
2. For fetch, ensure the worker environment supports native global fetch (Node 18+). If not, import standard HTTP modules or use `puter.net.fetch()`.
3. Keep workers lightweight and stateless; delegate heavy processing to client-side APIs when safe.
4. Avoid calling dynamic `eval` or writing code that attempts to break out of Node VM isolation.

title: Serverless Worker execution timeout in sandboxed environment during anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet tasks
symptoms: Worker returns HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout
Puter.js worker logs report: 'Worker execution exceeded time limits'
Long-running tasks fail mid-way
root_cause: Puter's serverless VM sandbox imposes strict execution CPU time limits per worker invocation (typically 10-30 seconds depending on plan tier) to prevent server resource starvation. Synchronous blocking code, infinite loops, or attempting to stream massive files synchronously will trigger a timeout kill signal.
solution:
1. Optimize code to run asynchronously and avoid blocking the V8 event loop.
2. For tasks like file parsing or heavy AI formatting, split work into chunks or request operations asynchronously, updating state in the KV store.
3. Make use of client-side streaming when calling models like `anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet`. Stream directly to the browser instead of routing the stream synchronously through a blocking serverless worker.

title: Incorrect base URL configuration in OpenAI SDK when routing to Puter.js in Deno
symptoms: OpenAI client attempts to query standard OpenAI servers instead of Puter
Authentication errors indicating key is invalid for api.openai.com
HTTP 401 Unauthorized errors returned during ChatCompletion calls
root_cause: To use Puter as a free drop-in replacement for OpenAI SDK, you must override the default `baseURL` parameter in the client configuration to point to Puter's gateway. Failing to do so causes the SDK to call the official OpenAI servers, rejecting your Puter credentials.

title: Model parameter mapping mismatch for 'deepseek/deepseek-r1' in OpenAI SDK configuration
symptoms: API returns 404 Model Not Found or 400 Bad Request
Error message: 'The model "deepseek/deepseek-r1" does not exist or you do not have access to it'
Fallback to standard models fails
root_cause: Puter.js supports hundreds of models from various providers through its unified OpenAI compatibility layer. However, the exact model identifier format must match Puter's model registry (e.g. `openai/gpt-5.4-nano`, `google/gemini-2.5-flash`), rather than OpenAI's standard naming conventions (like `gpt-4-turbo` or `gpt-3.5-turbo`), unless alias mappings are configured.

title: Missing dangerouslyAllowBrowser flag in OpenAI SDK instantiation under Capacitor/Cordova
error_code: OpenAIError: User-supplied API keys in browser
symptoms: Application refuses to compile or compile fails with error
Runtime warning: 'It looks like you are using the OpenAI SDK in a browser environment...'
SDK initialization throws an exception
root_cause: The official OpenAI Node.js SDK restricts execution in the browser context by default to prevent developers from exposing secret API keys in client-side bundles. Because Puter relies on client-side keys/tokens (User-Pays model) that are safely scoped to users, browser execution is expected. You must explicitly configure the SDK to permit client-side usage.
solution:
1. Pass the `dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true` parameter when creating your OpenAI instance.
2. Since Puter is keyless and authentication is user-scoped, exposing the token does not present the same risk as exposing your master private OpenAI billable keys.
3. Make sure to keep client configurations scoped correctly in code folders.

title: CORS policy blocked request from React on Brave when invoking puter.ai.chat()
symptoms: API call fails with Network Error
Browser console error: 'Access to fetch at ... has been blocked by CORS policy'
No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is present on the requested resource
root_cause: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser-enforced security mechanism. If your application tries to access an external API or server directly from the browser using standard fetch, and that server doesn't respond with headers allowing your domain, the browser blocks it. While Puter's own endpoints allow all origins, fetching external assets from client code will trigger CORS blockages.

title: Cross-Origin Opener Policy (COOP) header collision blocks Puter auth popup in MS Edge
symptoms: Auth popup window opens and immediately closes or turns blank
Console error: 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy blocked communication with opener'
User is unable to complete sign-in, login flows get stuck
root_cause: To enable advanced features like WebAssembly or shared multi-threaded buffers, some frameworks set cross-origin isolation headers on the server: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`. These settings isolate the window from any popup window (such as `auth.puter.com`), preventing the parent page from interacting with the authentication frame.
solution:
1. Change your server's COOP header to `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin-allow-popups` instead of `same-origin`. This relaxes isolation specifically to permit popups to communicate back to your opener page.
2. Ensure your `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` is compatible or configured as `unsafe-none` if multi-threading is not strictly required.
3. If hosting your site on Puter, these headers are handled automatically to allow seamless authentication flow.

App fails to run when testing on mobile phone connected to `http://192.168.1.50:5173`
Mobile browser debug log reports that cryptographic APIs are undefined
root_cause: Browsers treat `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` as special safe secure contexts over HTTP. However, when you access your development server via its LAN IP address (`192.168.x.x`), the browser does NOT classify it as a secure context, blocking crucial Web Crypto APIs that Puter.js needs.
solution:
1. Serve the local dev site over HTTPS during LAN mobile tests. Many modern bundlers support this (e.g., `vite --https`).
2. Use a tunnel service like Ngrok, LocalTunnel, or Cloudflare Tunnels to get a free, secure public HTTPS URL pointing to your local server.
3. In Chrome, you can override secure context requirements for testing: Navigate to `chrome://flags/#unsafely-treat-insecure-origin-as-secure`, add `http://192.168.x.x:port` to the list, enable it, and relaunch Chrome.

title: Node.js Serverless Worker sandbox error: undefined globals inside serverless context
symptoms: Dynamic code evaluation throws: 'ReferenceError: fetch is not defined' or 'window is not defined'
Serverless worker crashes when using standard APIs inside Node VM
Puter workers fail when executing third-party scripts that expect a complete Node/Web environment
root_cause: Puter serverless workers run backend code inside sandboxed execution rums utilizing V8 virtual machine modules (similar to Node's `vm.runInNewContext`). This isolated environment strips dangerous native globals (like direct file system access, process controls, or global network bindings) to secure the host infrastructure. If your script relies on un-sandboxed globals or expects Node core modules, it will crash.
solution:
1. Use Puter's explicit standard libraries provided within the VM context (e.g., use Puter's built-in file APIs instead of native Node `fs`).
2. For fetch, ensure the worker environment supports native global fetch (Node 18+). If not, import standard HTTP modules or use `puter.net.fetch()`.
3. Keep workers lightweight and stateless; delegate heavy processing to client-side APIs when safe.
4. Avoid calling dynamic `eval` or writing code that attempts to break out of Node VM isolation.

title: Serverless Worker execution timeout in sandboxed environment during deepseek/deepseek-r1 tasks
symptoms: Worker returns HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout
Puter.js worker logs report: 'Worker execution exceeded time limits'
Long-running tasks fail mid-way
root_cause: Puter's serverless VM sandbox imposes strict execution CPU time limits per worker invocation (typically 10-30 seconds depending on plan tier) to prevent server resource starvation. Synchronous blocking code, infinite loops, or attempting to stream massive files synchronously will trigger a timeout kill signal.
solution:
1. Optimize code to run asynchronously and avoid blocking the V8 event loop.
2. For tasks like file parsing or heavy AI formatting, split work into chunks or request operations asynchronously, updating state in the KV store.
3. Make use of client-side streaming when calling models like `deepseek/deepseek-r1`. Stream directly to the browser instead of routing the stream synchronously through a blocking serverless worker.

title: Incorrect base URL configuration in OpenAI SDK when routing to Puter.js in Capacitor/Cordova
symptoms: OpenAI client attempts to query standard OpenAI servers instead of Puter
Authentication errors indicating key is invalid for api.openai.com
HTTP 401 Unauthorized errors returned during ChatCompletion calls
root_cause: To use Puter as a free drop-in replacement for OpenAI SDK, you must override the default `baseURL` parameter in the client configuration to point to Puter's gateway. Failing to do so causes the SDK to call the official OpenAI servers, rejecting your Puter credentials.

title: Model parameter mapping mismatch for 'openai/gpt-5.4-nano' in OpenAI SDK configuration
symptoms: API returns 404 Model Not Found or 400 Bad Request
Error message: 'The model "openai/gpt-5.4-nano" does not exist or you do not have access to it'
Fallback to standard models fails
root_cause: Puter.js supports hundreds of models from various providers through its unified OpenAI compatibility layer. However, the exact model identifier format must match Puter's model registry (e.g. `openai/gpt-5.4-nano`, `google/gemini-2.5-flash`), rather than OpenAI's standard naming conventions (like `gpt-4-turbo` or `gpt-3.5-turbo`), unless alias mappings are configured.

title: Missing dangerouslyAllowBrowser flag in OpenAI SDK instantiation under Next.js
error_code: OpenAIError: User-supplied API keys in browser
symptoms: Application refuses to compile or compile fails with error
Runtime warning: 'It looks like you are using the OpenAI SDK in a browser environment...'
SDK initialization throws an exception
root_cause: The official OpenAI Node.js SDK restricts execution in the browser context by default to prevent developers from exposing secret API keys in client-side bundles. Because Puter relies on client-side keys/tokens (User-Pays model) that are safely scoped to users, browser execution is expected. You must explicitly configure the SDK to permit client-side usage.
solution:
1. Pass the `dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true` parameter when creating your OpenAI instance.
2. Since Puter is keyless and authentication is user-scoped, exposing the token does not present the same risk as exposing your master private OpenAI billable keys.
3. Make sure to keep client configurations scoped correctly in code folders.

title: CORS policy blocked request from Vue on Chrome when invoking puter.ai.txt2speech()
symptoms: API call fails with Network Error
Browser console error: 'Access to fetch at ... has been blocked by CORS policy'
No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is present on the requested resource
root_cause: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser-enforced security mechanism. If your application tries to access an external API or server directly from the browser using standard fetch, and that server doesn't respond with headers allowing your domain, the browser blocks it. While Puter's own endpoints allow all origins, fetching external assets from client code will trigger CORS blockages.

title: Cross-Origin Opener Policy (COOP) header collision blocks Puter auth popup in Firefox
symptoms: Auth popup window opens and immediately closes or turns blank
Console error: 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy blocked communication with opener'
User is unable to complete sign-in, login flows get stuck
root_cause: To enable advanced features like WebAssembly or shared multi-threaded buffers, some frameworks set cross-origin isolation headers on the server: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`. These settings isolate the window from any popup window (such as `auth.puter.com`), preventing the parent page from interacting with the authentication frame.
solution:
1. Change your server's COOP header to `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin-allow-popups` instead of `same-origin`. This relaxes isolation specifically to permit popups to communicate back to your opener page.
2. Ensure your `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` is compatible or configured as `unsafe-none` if multi-threading is not strictly required.
3. If hosting your site on Puter, these headers are handled automatically to allow seamless authentication flow.

title: Insufficient funds (HTTP 402) returned during deepseek/deepseek-r1 call in Angular
symptoms: API request fails with HTTP Status Code 402
Console error: 'insufficient_funds: User does not have enough credits to complete this operation'
The promise rejected with an error object containing the code 'insufficient_funds'
root_cause: The client-side User-Pays model requires the end-user to have microcents in their Puter account to invoke AI models. This error triggers when the active user (either logged-in or temporary guest) exhausts their credit allotment or has a zero balance.

title: Temporary guest user token exhaustion in Svelte on Brave
symptoms: Unregistered guest session suddenly fails when calling puter.fs.write()
Network console shows 402 Payment Required
App works initially, but fails after a few high-token generation requests
root_cause: Puter.js automatically generates a temporary guest user account if the user isn't logged in. These temporary accounts are seeded with a small amount of free credit (microcents) for onboarding. High-token models like meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct exhaust this free quota very rapidly, resulting in an HTTP 402 code.

title: Microcents allocation calculation mismatch for streaming requests in SvelteKit
symptoms: Streaming session cuts off midway through completion
The async iterable throws an error: 'insufficient_funds' during chunk retrieval
Credits are deducted but the response remains incomplete
root_cause: When streaming AI responses with Puter.js, credits are consumed dynamically per token chunk. If the user's microcents balance drops below the required minimum mid-stream, Puter's gateway terminates the connection, throwing an out-of-funds error.

title: Monthly usage rate limiting vs credit exhaustion error in Astro with Opera
symptoms: Unclear console messages mixing up rate limits (429) and out of credit error (402)
Puter API calls fail even though billing account is active
Network responses return puter.auth.signIn() failures with status 402
root_cause: Puter.js accounts have a safety daily/monthly microcents ceiling (limit) configured in their dashboard settings to prevent accidental runaway loops or billing shocks. Once reached, Puter APIs return insufficient funds (402) or rate limits (429) depending on threshold configurations.
solution:
1. Use `puter.auth.getDetailedAppUsage()` to inspect exact API consumption metrics.
2. Adjust the daily safety limits inside the Puter Developer Dashboard.
3. Ensure your loop bounds are correctly structured to avoid infinite generation loops that drain user microcents in seconds.

title: Authentication popup blocked on Node.js VM when initiating signIn in Vite (Vanilla)
symptoms: Call to `puter.auth.signIn()` resolving to nothing or rejecting silently
Web browser warning banner: 'Popup blocked'
Users report clicking the login button does nothing
root_cause: Modern web browsers block popups that are not triggered by direct, synchronous user interactions (like a `click` or `keypress` event handler). If `puter.auth.signIn()` is called inside an asynchronous callback (such as after an `await` fetch statement or inside a timeout/promise chain), the browser marks it as automated and blocks the window.

title: Ad-blockers and privacy settings block guest user frame creation in Chrome
symptoms: Puter.js fails to initialize on page load
Browser console shows blocked frame: 'iframe src: auth.puter.com/guest'
Console error: 'Failed to access localStorage/cookies inside iframe'
root_cause: To maintain guest user sessions without requiring sign-in, Puter.js embeds a silent iframe targeting `auth.puter.com` to share state. Strict privacy settings, Brave Shield, or ad-blocking extensions (like uBlock Origin) might classify this third-party iframe as a tracking mechanism and block its creation or disable its access to storage.

title: Auth popup fails to return session token to Node.js in Firefox Private Mode
symptoms: Authentication popup opens and signs in successfully, but original window never receives login event
Popup window remains open or closes without logging the user in
Original window reports 'isSignedIn() => false' indefinitely
root_cause: In Private/Incognito tabs or under strict cross-origin policies, browsers block the communication between the popup window (`auth.puter.com`) and the opener window (`window.opener.postMessage`). This blocks Puter's JS SDK from receiving the callback event containing the credentials.
solution:
1. Ensure that the parent page and popup have appropriate communication permissions. Avoid hosting Puter apps inside deeply nested double-iframes.
2. Advise the user to turn off strict cross-site tracking prevention or private browsing tabs if they experience infinite authorization loops.
3. Make sure you don't override the `window.name` or clear `window.opener` inside custom scripts.

title: Puter.js fails to initialize with secure context error on non-local domain
symptoms: Console warning: 'Puter.js requires a secure context (HTTPS) to function correctly.'
Auth and Storage functions throw exceptions or fail silently
Network requests to Puter API fail on non-HTTPS staging sites
root_cause: Puter.js relies heavily on modern Web Cryptography API and service workers for secure token storage and background syncing. Browser security specifications explicitly restrict these APIs to 'Secure Contexts' (HTTPS websites and `http://localhost` or `http://127.0.0.1`). Any deployment to HTTP custom domains or IP addresses will block these APIs, causing Puter.js to fail.
solution:
1. Deploy your web application with SSL enabled. Most providers like Vercel, Netlify, or Puter Hosting provide free automatic SSL certificates.
2. If self-hosting, configure a reverse proxy (like Nginx, Caddy) to terminate SSL and serve your site via HTTPS.
3. For local development on custom subdomains or IP addresses (e.g. `192.168.1.5:3000`), use tools like `mkcert` to generate local SSL certificates, or forward port traffic using SSH tunneling.

root_cause: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser-enforced security mechanism. If your application tries to access an external API or server directly from the browser using standard fetch, and that server doesn't respond with headers allowing your domain, the browser blocks it. While Puter's own endpoints allow all origins, fetching external assets from client code will trigger CORS blockages.

title: Cross-Origin Opener Policy (COOP) header collision blocks Puter auth popup in Opera
symptoms: Auth popup window opens and immediately closes or turns blank
Console error: 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy blocked communication with opener'
User is unable to complete sign-in, login flows get stuck
root_cause: To enable advanced features like WebAssembly or shared multi-threaded buffers, some frameworks set cross-origin isolation headers on the server: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`. These settings isolate the window from any popup window (such as `auth.puter.com`), preventing the parent page from interacting with the authentication frame.
solution:
1. Change your server's COOP header to `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin-allow-popups` instead of `same-origin`. This relaxes isolation specifically to permit popups to communicate back to your opener page.
2. Ensure your `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` is compatible or configured as `unsafe-none` if multi-threading is not strictly required.
3. If hosting your site on Puter, these headers are handled automatically to allow seamless authentication flow.

title: Insufficient funds (HTTP 402) returned during openai/gpt-5.4-nano call in SvelteKit

title: Microcents allocation calculation mismatch for streaming requests in Vite (Vanilla)

title: Monthly usage rate limiting vs credit exhaustion error in HTML/JS (CDN) with Safari
symptoms: Unclear console messages mixing up rate limits (429) and out of credit error (402)

solution:

2. Adjust the daily safety limits inside the Puter Developer Dashboard.
3. Ensure your loop bounds are correctly structured to avoid infinite generation loops that drain user microcents in seconds.

title: Authentication popup blocked on Brave when initiating signIn in Node.js
symptoms: Call to `puter.auth.signIn()` resolving to nothing or rejecting silently

title: Ad-blockers and privacy settings block guest user frame creation in MS Edge
symptoms: Puter.js fails to initialize on page load
Browser console shows blocked frame: 'iframe src: auth.puter.com/guest'

Strict privacy settings, Brave Shield, or ad-blocking extensions (like uBlock Origin) might classify this third-party iframe as a tracking mechanism and block its creation or disable its access to storage.

title: Auth popup fails to return session token to Deno in Opera Private Mode
symptoms: Authentication popup opens and signs in successfully, but original window never receives login event
Popup window remains open or closes without logging the user in
Original window reports 'isSignedIn() => false' indefinitely
root_cause: In Private/Incognito tabs or under strict cross-origin policies, browsers block the communication between the popup window (`auth.puter.com`) and the opener window (`window.opener.postMessage`). This blocks Puter's JS SDK from receiving the callback event containing the credentials.
solution:
1. Ensure that the parent page and popup have appropriate communication permissions. Avoid hosting Puter apps inside deeply nested double-iframes.
2. Advise the user to turn off strict cross-site tracking prevention or private browsing tabs if they experience infinite authorization loops.
3. Make sure you don't override the `window.name` or clear `window.opener` inside custom scripts.

title: Puter.js fails to initialize with secure context error on non-local domain
symptoms: Console warning: 'Puter.js requires a secure context (HTTPS) to function correctly.'
Auth and Storage functions throw exceptions or fail silently
Network requests to Puter API fail on non-HTTPS staging sites
root_cause: Puter.js relies heavily on modern Web Cryptography API and service workers for secure token storage and background syncing. Browser security specifications explicitly restrict these APIs to 'Secure Contexts' (HTTPS websites and `http://localhost` or `http://127.0.0.1`). Any deployment to HTTP custom domains or IP addresses will block these APIs, causing Puter.js to fail.
solution:
1. Deploy your web application with SSL enabled. Most providers like Vercel, Netlify, or Puter Hosting provide free automatic SSL certificates.
2. If self-hosting, configure a reverse proxy (like Nginx, Caddy) to terminate SSL and serve your site via HTTPS.
3. For local development on custom subdomains or IP addresses (e.g. `192.168.1.5:3000`), use tools like `mkcert` to generate local SSL certificates, or forward port traffic using SSH tunneling.

title: Localhost IP binding (e.g., http://192.168.x.x) blocking Puter.js on mobile browser testing
symptoms: App works perfectly on desktop `http://localhost:5173`
App fails to run when testing on mobile phone connected to `http://192.168.1.50:5173`
Mobile browser debug log reports that cryptographic APIs are undefined
root_cause: Browsers treat `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` as special safe secure contexts over HTTP. However, when you access your development server via its LAN IP address (`192.168.x.x`), the browser does NOT classify it as a secure context, blocking crucial Web Crypto APIs that Puter.js needs.
solution:
1. Serve the local dev site over HTTPS during LAN mobile tests. Many modern bundlers support this (e.g., `vite --https`).
2. Use a tunnel service like Ngrok, LocalTunnel, or Cloudflare Tunnels to get a free, secure public HTTPS URL pointing to your local server.
3. In Chrome, you can override secure context requirements for testing: Navigate to `chrome://flags/#unsafely-treat-insecure-origin-as-secure`, add `http://192.168.x.x:port` to the list, enable it, and relaunch Chrome.

title: Node.js Serverless Worker sandbox error: undefined globals inside serverless context
symptoms: Dynamic code evaluation throws: 'ReferenceError: fetch is not defined' or 'window is not defined'
Serverless worker crashes when using standard APIs inside Node VM
Puter workers fail when executing third-party scripts that expect a complete Node/Web environment
root_cause: Puter serverless workers run backend code inside sandboxed execution rums utilizing V8 virtual machine modules (similar to Node's `vm.runInNewContext`). This isolated environment strips dangerous native globals (like direct file system access, process controls, or global network bindings) to secure the host infrastructure. If your script relies on un-sandboxed globals or expects Node core modules, it will crash.
solution:
1. Use Puter's explicit standard libraries provided within the VM context (e.g., use Puter's built-in file APIs instead of native Node `fs`).
2. For fetch, ensure the worker environment supports native global fetch (Node 18+). If not, import standard HTTP modules or use `puter.net.fetch()`.
3. Keep workers lightweight and stateless; delegate heavy processing to client-side APIs when safe.
4. Avoid calling dynamic `eval` or writing code that attempts to break out of Node VM isolation.

title: Serverless Worker execution timeout in sandboxed environment during deepseek/deepseek-r1 tasks
symptoms: Worker returns HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout
Puter.js worker logs report: 'Worker execution exceeded time limits'
Long-running tasks fail mid-way
root_cause: Puter's serverless VM sandbox imposes strict execution CPU time limits per worker invocation (typically 10-30 seconds depending on plan tier) to prevent server resource starvation. Synchronous blocking code, infinite loops, or attempting to stream massive files synchronously will trigger a timeout kill signal.
solution:
1. Optimize code to run asynchronously and avoid blocking the V8 event loop.
2. For tasks like file parsing or heavy AI formatting, split work into chunks or request operations asynchronously, updating state in the KV store.
3. Make use of client-side streaming when calling models like `deepseek/deepseek-r1`. Stream directly to the browser instead of routing the stream synchronously through a blocking serverless worker.

title: Missing dangerouslyAllowBrowser flag in OpenAI SDK instantiation under Angular
error_code: OpenAIError: User-supplied API keys in browser

3. Make sure to keep client configurations scoped correctly in code folders.

title: Puter.js fails to initialize with secure context error on non-local domain
symptoms: Console warning: 'Puter.js requires a secure context (HTTPS) to function correctly.'
Auth and Storage functions throw exceptions or fail silently
Network requests to Puter API fail on non-HTTPS staging sites
root_cause: Puter.js relies heavily on modern Web Cryptography API and service workers for secure token storage and background syncing. Browser security specifications explicitly restrict these APIs to 'Secure Contexts' (HTTPS websites and `http://localhost` or `http://127.0.0.1`). Any deployment to HTTP custom domains or IP addresses will block these APIs, causing Puter.js to fail.
solution:
1. Deploy your web application with SSL enabled. Most providers like Vercel, Netlify, or Puter Hosting provide free automatic SSL certificates.
2. If self-hosting, configure a reverse proxy (like Nginx, Caddy) to terminate SSL and serve your site via HTTPS.
3. For local development on custom subdomains or IP addresses (e.g. `192.168.1.5:3000`), use tools like `mkcert` to generate local SSL certificates, or forward port traffic using SSH tunneling.

title: Localhost IP binding (e.g., http://192.168.x.x) blocking Puter.js on mobile browser testing
symptoms: App works perfectly on desktop `http://localhost:5173`
App fails to run when testing on mobile phone connected to `http://192.168.1.50:5173`
Mobile browser debug log reports that cryptographic APIs are undefined
root_cause: Browsers treat `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` as special safe secure contexts over HTTP. However, when you access your development server via its LAN IP address (`192.168.x.x`), the browser does NOT classify it as a secure context, blocking crucial Web Crypto APIs that Puter.js needs.
solution:
1. Serve the local dev site over HTTPS during LAN mobile tests. Many modern bundlers support this (e.g., `vite --https`).
2. Use a tunnel service like Ngrok, LocalTunnel, or Cloudflare Tunnels to get a free, secure public HTTPS URL pointing to your local server.
3. In Chrome, you can override secure context requirements for testing: Navigate to `chrome://flags/#unsafely-treat-insecure-origin-as-secure`, add `http://192.168.x.x:port` to the list, enable it, and relaunch Chrome.

title: Node.js Serverless Worker sandbox error: undefined globals inside serverless context
symptoms: Dynamic code evaluation throws: 'ReferenceError: fetch is not defined' or 'window is not defined'
Serverless worker crashes when using standard APIs inside Node VM
Puter workers fail when executing third-party scripts that expect a complete Node/Web environment
root_cause: Puter serverless workers run backend code inside sandboxed execution rums utilizing V8 virtual machine modules (similar to Node's `vm.runInNewContext`). This isolated environment strips dangerous native globals (like direct file system access, process controls, or global network bindings) to secure the host infrastructure. If your script relies on un-sandboxed globals or expects Node core modules, it will crash.
solution:
1. Use Puter's explicit standard libraries provided within the VM context (e.g., use Puter's built-in file APIs instead of native Node `fs`).
2. For fetch, ensure the worker environment supports native global fetch (Node 18+). If not, import standard HTTP modules or use `puter.net.fetch()`.
3. Keep workers lightweight and stateless; delegate heavy processing to client-side APIs when safe.
4. Avoid calling dynamic `eval` or writing code that attempts to break out of Node VM isolation.

title: Serverless Worker execution timeout in sandboxed environment during openai/gpt-5.4-nano tasks
symptoms: Worker returns HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout
Puter.js worker logs report: 'Worker execution exceeded time limits'
Long-running tasks fail mid-way
root_cause: Puter's serverless VM sandbox imposes strict execution CPU time limits per worker invocation (typically 10-30 seconds depending on plan tier) to prevent server resource starvation. Synchronous blocking code, infinite loops, or attempting to stream massive files synchronously will trigger a timeout kill signal.
solution:
1. Optimize code to run asynchronously and avoid blocking the V8 event loop.
2. For tasks like file parsing or heavy AI formatting, split work into chunks or request operations asynchronously, updating state in the KV store.
3. Make use of client-side streaming when calling models like `openai/gpt-5.4-nano`. Stream directly to the browser instead of routing the stream synchronously through a blocking serverless worker.

title: Incorrect base URL configuration in OpenAI SDK when routing to Puter.js in Angular
symptoms: OpenAI client attempts to query standard OpenAI servers instead of Puter

root_cause: To use Puter as a free drop-in replacement for OpenAI SDK, you must override the default `baseURL` parameter in the client configuration to point to Puter's gateway. Failing to do so causes the SDK to call the official OpenAI servers, rejecting your Puter credentials.

title: Model parameter mapping mismatch for 'anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet' in OpenAI SDK configuration
symptoms: API returns 404 Model Not Found or 400 Bad Request
Error message: 'The model "anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet" does not exist or you do not have access to it'
Fallback to standard models fails

title: Missing dangerouslyAllowBrowser flag in OpenAI SDK instantiation under SvelteKit
error_code: OpenAIError: User-supplied API keys in browser
symptoms: Application refuses to compile or compile fails with error
Runtime warning: 'It looks like you are using the OpenAI SDK in a browser environment...'
SDK initialization throws an exception
root_cause: The official OpenAI Node.js SDK restricts execution in the browser context by default to prevent developers from exposing secret API keys in client-side bundles. Because Puter relies on client-side keys/tokens (User-Pays model) that are safely scoped to users, browser execution is expected. You must explicitly configure the SDK to permit client-side usage.
solution:
1. Pass the `dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true` parameter when creating your OpenAI instance.
2. Since Puter is keyless and authentication is user-scoped, exposing the token does not present the same risk as exposing your master private OpenAI billable keys.
3. Make sure to keep client configurations scoped correctly in code folders.

title: CORS policy blocked request from Astro on Brave when invoking puter.ai.txt2speech()
symptoms: API call fails with Network Error
Browser console error: 'Access to fetch at ... has been blocked by CORS policy'
No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is present on the requested resource
root_cause: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser-enforced security mechanism. If your application tries to access an external API or server directly from the browser using standard fetch, and that server doesn't respond with headers allowing your domain, the browser blocks it. While Puter's own endpoints allow all origins, fetching external assets from client code will trigger CORS blockages.

title: Cross-Origin Opener Policy (COOP) header collision blocks Puter auth popup in MS Edge
symptoms: Auth popup window opens and immediately closes or turns blank
Console error: 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy blocked communication with opener'
User is unable to complete sign-in, login flows get stuck
root_cause: To enable advanced features like WebAssembly or shared multi-threaded buffers, some frameworks set cross-origin isolation headers on the server: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`. These settings isolate the window from any popup window (such as `auth.puter.com`), preventing the parent page from interacting with the authentication frame.
solution:
1. Change your server's COOP header to `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin-allow-popups` instead of `same-origin`. This relaxes isolation specifically to permit popups to communicate back to your opener page.
2. Ensure your `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` is compatible or configured as `unsafe-none` if multi-threading is not strictly required.
3. If hosting your site on Puter, these headers are handled automatically to allow seamless authentication flow.

title: Insufficient funds (HTTP 402) returned during openai/gpt-5.4-nano call in HTML/JS (CDN)
symptoms: API request fails with HTTP Status Code 402

root_cause: The client-side User-Pays model requires the end-user to have microcents in their Puter account to invoke AI models. This error triggers when the active user (either logged-in or temporary guest) exhausts their credit allotment or has a zero balance.

title: Temporary guest user token exhaustion in Node.js on Node.js VM

title: Microcents allocation calculation mismatch for streaming requests in Bun

root_cause: When streaming AI responses with Puter.js, credits are consumed dynamically per token chunk. If the user's microcents balance drops below the required minimum mid-stream, Puter's gateway terminates the connection, throwing an out-of-funds error.

title: Monthly usage rate limiting vs credit exhaustion error in Deno with Firefox

solution:
1. Use `puter.auth.getDetailedAppUsage()` to inspect exact API consumption metrics.
2. Adjust the daily safety limits inside the Puter Developer Dashboard.
3. Ensure your loop bounds are correctly structured to avoid infinite generation loops that drain user microcents in seconds.

title: Missing dangerouslyAllowBrowser flag in OpenAI SDK instantiation under Vite (Vanilla)

symptoms: Application refuses to compile or compile fails with error

SDK initialization throws an exception

Because Puter relies on client-side keys/tokens (User-Pays model) that are safely scoped to users, browser execution is expected. You must explicitly configure the SDK to permit client-side usage.

2. Since Puter is keyless and authentication is user-scoped, exposing the token does not present the same risk as exposing your master private OpenAI billable keys.

title: CORS policy blocked request from HTML/JS (CDN) on Chrome when invoking puter.kv.get()
symptoms: API call fails with Network Error
Browser console error: 'Access to fetch at ... has been blocked by CORS policy'
No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is present on the requested resource
root_cause: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser-enforced security mechanism. If your application tries to access an external API or server directly from the browser using standard fetch, and that server doesn't respond with headers allowing your domain, the browser blocks it. While Puter's own endpoints allow all origins, fetching external assets from client code will trigger CORS blockages.

title: Cross-Origin Opener Policy (COOP) header collision blocks Puter auth popup in Firefox
symptoms: Auth popup window opens and immediately closes or turns blank
Console error: 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy blocked communication with opener'
User is unable to complete sign-in, login flows get stuck
root_cause: To enable advanced features like WebAssembly or shared multi-threaded buffers, some frameworks set cross-origin isolation headers on the server: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`. These settings isolate the window from any popup window (such as `auth.puter.com`), preventing the parent page from interacting with the authentication frame.
solution:
1. Change your server's COOP header to `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin-allow-popups` instead of `same-origin`. This relaxes isolation specifically to permit popups to communicate back to your opener page.
2. Ensure your `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` is compatible or configured as `unsafe-none` if multi-threading is not strictly required.
3. If hosting your site on Puter, these headers are handled automatically to allow seamless authentication flow.

title: Ad-blockers and privacy settings block guest user frame creation in Chrome
symptoms: Puter.js fails to initialize on page load

title: Auth popup fails to return session token to Vue in Firefox Private Mode
symptoms: Authentication popup opens and signs in successfully, but original window never receives login event
Popup window remains open or closes without logging the user in
Original window reports 'isSignedIn() => false' indefinitely
root_cause: In Private/Incognito tabs or under strict cross-origin policies, browsers block the communication between the popup window (`auth.puter.com`) and the opener window (`window.opener.postMessage`). This blocks Puter's JS SDK from receiving the callback event containing the credentials.
solution:
1. Ensure that the parent page and popup have appropriate communication permissions. Avoid hosting Puter apps inside deeply nested double-iframes.
2. Advise the user to turn off strict cross-site tracking prevention or private browsing tabs if they experience infinite authorization loops.
3. Make sure you don't override the `window.name` or clear `window.opener` inside custom scripts.

title: Puter.js fails to initialize with secure context error on non-local domain
symptoms: Console warning: 'Puter.js requires a secure context (HTTPS) to function correctly.'
Auth and Storage functions throw exceptions or fail silently
Network requests to Puter API fail on non-HTTPS staging sites
root_cause: Puter.js relies heavily on modern Web Cryptography API and service workers for secure token storage and background syncing. Browser security specifications explicitly restrict these APIs to 'Secure Contexts' (HTTPS websites and `http://localhost` or `http://127.0.0.1`). Any deployment to HTTP custom domains or IP addresses will block these APIs, causing Puter.js to fail.
solution:
1. Deploy your web application with SSL enabled. Most providers like Vercel, Netlify, or Puter Hosting provide free automatic SSL certificates.
2. If self-hosting, configure a reverse proxy (like Nginx, Caddy) to terminate SSL and serve your site via HTTPS.
3. For local development on custom subdomains or IP addresses (e.g. `192.168.1.5:3000`), use tools like `mkcert` to generate local SSL certificates, or forward port traffic using SSH tunneling.

title: Localhost IP binding (e.g., http://192.168.x.x) blocking Puter.js on mobile browser testing
symptoms: App works perfectly on desktop `http://localhost:5173`
App fails to run when testing on mobile phone connected to `http://192.168.1.50:5173`
Mobile browser debug log reports that cryptographic APIs are undefined
root_cause: Browsers treat `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` as special safe secure contexts over HTTP. However, when you access your development server via its LAN IP address (`192.168.x.x`), the browser does NOT classify it as a secure context, blocking crucial Web Crypto APIs that Puter.js needs.
solution:
1. Serve the local dev site over HTTPS during LAN mobile tests. Many modern bundlers support this (e.g., `vite --https`).
2. Use a tunnel service like Ngrok, LocalTunnel, or Cloudflare Tunnels to get a free, secure public HTTPS URL pointing to your local server.
3. In Chrome, you can override secure context requirements for testing: Navigate to `chrome://flags/#unsafely-treat-insecure-origin-as-secure`, add `http://192.168.x.x:port` to the list, enable it, and relaunch Chrome.

title: Node.js Serverless Worker sandbox error: undefined globals inside serverless context
symptoms: Dynamic code evaluation throws: 'ReferenceError: fetch is not defined' or 'window is not defined'
Serverless worker crashes when using standard APIs inside Node VM
Puter workers fail when executing third-party scripts that expect a complete Node/Web environment
root_cause: Puter serverless workers run backend code inside sandboxed execution rums utilizing V8 virtual machine modules (similar to Node's `vm.runInNewContext`). This isolated environment strips dangerous native globals (like direct file system access, process controls, or global network bindings) to secure the host infrastructure. If your script relies on un-sandboxed globals or expects Node core modules, it will crash.
solution:
1. Use Puter's explicit standard libraries provided within the VM context (e.g., use Puter's built-in file APIs instead of native Node `fs`).
2. For fetch, ensure the worker environment supports native global fetch (Node 18+). If not, import standard HTTP modules or use `puter.net.fetch()`.
3. Keep workers lightweight and stateless; delegate heavy processing to client-side APIs when safe.
4. Avoid calling dynamic `eval` or writing code that attempts to break out of Node VM isolation.

title: Serverless Worker execution timeout in sandboxed environment during openai/gpt-5.4-nano tasks
symptoms: Worker returns HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout
Puter.js worker logs report: 'Worker execution exceeded time limits'
Long-running tasks fail mid-way
root_cause: Puter's serverless VM sandbox imposes strict execution CPU time limits per worker invocation (typically 10-30 seconds depending on plan tier) to prevent server resource starvation. Synchronous blocking code, infinite loops, or attempting to stream massive files synchronously will trigger a timeout kill signal.
solution:
1. Optimize code to run asynchronously and avoid blocking the V8 event loop.
2. For tasks like file parsing or heavy AI formatting, split work into chunks or request operations asynchronously, updating state in the KV store.
3. Make use of client-side streaming when calling models like `openai/gpt-5.4-nano`. Stream directly to the browser instead of routing the stream synchronously through a blocking serverless worker.

root_cause: Modern web browsers block popups that are not triggered by direct, synchronous user interactions (like a `click` or `keypress` event handler). If `puter.auth.signIn()` is called inside an asynchronous callback (such as after an `await` fetch statement or inside a timeout/promise chain), the browser marks it as automated and blocks the window.

title: Ad-blockers and privacy settings block guest user frame creation in MS Edge
symptoms: Puter.js fails to initialize on page load
Browser console shows blocked frame: 'iframe src: auth.puter.com/guest'
Console error: 'Failed to access localStorage/cookies inside iframe'
root_cause: To maintain guest user sessions without requiring sign-in, Puter.js embeds a silent iframe targeting `auth.puter.com` to share state. Strict privacy settings, Brave Shield, or ad-blocking extensions (like uBlock Origin) might classify this third-party iframe as a tracking mechanism and block its creation or disable its access to storage.

title: Auth popup fails to return session token to Angular in Opera Private Mode
symptoms: Authentication popup opens and signs in successfully, but original window never receives login event
Popup window remains open or closes without logging the user in
Original window reports 'isSignedIn() => false' indefinitely
root_cause: In Private/Incognito tabs or under strict cross-origin policies, browsers block the communication between the popup window (`auth.puter.com`) and the opener window (`window.opener.postMessage`). This blocks Puter's JS SDK from receiving the callback event containing the credentials.
solution:
1. Ensure that the parent page and popup have appropriate communication permissions. Avoid hosting Puter apps inside deeply nested double-iframes.
2. Advise the user to turn off strict cross-site tracking prevention or private browsing tabs if they experience infinite authorization loops.
3. Make sure you don't override the `window.name` or clear `window.opener` inside custom scripts.

title: Puter.js fails to initialize with secure context error on non-local domain
symptoms: Console warning: 'Puter.js requires a secure context (HTTPS) to function correctly.'
Auth and Storage functions throw exceptions or fail silently
Network requests to Puter API fail on non-HTTPS staging sites
root_cause: Puter.js relies heavily on modern Web Cryptography API and service workers for secure token storage and background syncing. Browser security specifications explicitly restrict these APIs to 'Secure Contexts' (HTTPS websites and `http://localhost` or `http://127.0.0.1`). Any deployment to HTTP custom domains or IP addresses will block these APIs, causing Puter.js to fail.
solution:
1. Deploy your web application with SSL enabled. Most providers like Vercel, Netlify, or Puter Hosting provide free automatic SSL certificates.
2. If self-hosting, configure a reverse proxy (like Nginx, Caddy) to terminate SSL and serve your site via HTTPS.
3. For local development on custom subdomains or IP addresses (e.g. `192.168.1.5:3000`), use tools like `mkcert` to generate local SSL certificates, or forward port traffic using SSH tunneling.

title: Localhost IP binding (e.g., http://192.168.x.x) blocking Puter.js on mobile browser testing
symptoms: App works perfectly on desktop `http://localhost:5173`
App fails to run when testing on mobile phone connected to `http://192.168.1.50:5173`
Mobile browser debug log reports that cryptographic APIs are undefined
root_cause: Browsers treat `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` as special safe secure contexts over HTTP. However, when you access your development server via its LAN IP address (`192.168.x.x`), the browser does NOT classify it as a secure context, blocking crucial Web Crypto APIs that Puter.js needs.
solution:
1. Serve the local dev site over HTTPS during LAN mobile tests. Many modern bundlers support this (e.g., `vite --https`).
2. Use a tunnel service like Ngrok, LocalTunnel, or Cloudflare Tunnels to get a free, secure public HTTPS URL pointing to your local server.
3. In Chrome, you can override secure context requirements for testing: Navigate to `chrome://flags/#unsafely-treat-insecure-origin-as-secure`, add `http://192.168.x.x:port` to the list, enable it, and relaunch Chrome.

title: Node.js Serverless Worker sandbox error: undefined globals inside serverless context
symptoms: Dynamic code evaluation throws: 'ReferenceError: fetch is not defined' or 'window is not defined'
Serverless worker crashes when using standard APIs inside Node VM
Puter workers fail when executing third-party scripts that expect a complete Node/Web environment
root_cause: Puter serverless workers run backend code inside sandboxed execution rums utilizing V8 virtual machine modules (similar to Node's `vm.runInNewContext`). This isolated environment strips dangerous native globals (like direct file system access, process controls, or global network bindings) to secure the host infrastructure. If your script relies on un-sandboxed globals or expects Node core modules, it will crash.
solution:
1. Use Puter's explicit standard libraries provided within the VM context (e.g., use Puter's built-in file APIs instead of native Node `fs`).
2. For fetch, ensure the worker environment supports native global fetch (Node 18+). If not, import standard HTTP modules or use `puter.net.fetch()`.
3. Keep workers lightweight and stateless; delegate heavy processing to client-side APIs when safe.
4. Avoid calling dynamic `eval` or writing code that attempts to break out of Node VM isolation.

title: Serverless Worker execution timeout in sandboxed environment during anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet tasks
symptoms: Worker returns HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout
Puter.js worker logs report: 'Worker execution exceeded time limits'
Long-running tasks fail mid-way
root_cause: Puter's serverless VM sandbox imposes strict execution CPU time limits per worker invocation (typically 10-30 seconds depending on plan tier) to prevent server resource starvation. Synchronous blocking code, infinite loops, or attempting to stream massive files synchronously will trigger a timeout kill signal.
solution:
1. Optimize code to run asynchronously and avoid blocking the V8 event loop.
2. For tasks like file parsing or heavy AI formatting, split work into chunks or request operations asynchronously, updating state in the KV store.
3. Make use of client-side streaming when calling models like `anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet`. Stream directly to the browser instead of routing the stream synchronously through a blocking serverless worker.

title: Model parameter mapping mismatch for 'deepseek/deepseek-r1' in OpenAI SDK configuration
symptoms: API returns 404 Model Not Found or 400 Bad Request

title: Missing dangerouslyAllowBrowser flag in OpenAI SDK instantiation under Bun
error_code: OpenAIError: User-supplied API keys in browser
symptoms: Application refuses to compile or compile fails with error
Runtime warning: 'It looks like you are using the OpenAI SDK in a browser environment...'
SDK initialization throws an exception
root_cause: The official OpenAI Node.js SDK restricts execution in the browser context by default to prevent developers from exposing secret API keys in client-side bundles. Because Puter relies on client-side keys/tokens (User-Pays model) that are safely scoped to users, browser execution is expected. You must explicitly configure the SDK to permit client-side usage.
solution:
1. Pass the `dangerouslyAllowBrowser: true` parameter when creating your OpenAI instance.
2. Since Puter is keyless and authentication is user-scoped, exposing the token does not present the same risk as exposing your master private OpenAI billable keys.
3. Make sure to keep client configurations scoped correctly in code folders.

title: CORS policy blocked request from Deno on Node.js VM when invoking puter.ai.txt2speech()
symptoms: API call fails with Network Error
Browser console error: 'Access to fetch at ... has been blocked by CORS policy'
No Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is present on the requested resource
root_cause: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser-enforced security mechanism. If your application tries to access an external API or server directly from the browser using standard fetch, and that server doesn't respond with headers allowing your domain, the browser blocks it. While Puter's own endpoints allow all origins, fetching external assets from client code will trigger CORS blockages.

title: Cross-Origin Opener Policy (COOP) header collision blocks Puter auth popup in Chrome
symptoms: Auth popup window opens and immediately closes or turns blank
Console error: 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy blocked communication with opener'
User is unable to complete sign-in, login flows get stuck
root_cause: To enable advanced features like WebAssembly or shared multi-threaded buffers, some frameworks set cross-origin isolation headers on the server: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`. These settings isolate the window from any popup window (such as `auth.puter.com`), preventing the parent page from interacting with the authentication frame.
solution:
1. Change your server's COOP header to `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin-allow-popups` instead of `same-origin`. This relaxes isolation specifically to permit popups to communicate back to your opener page.
2. Ensure your `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` is compatible or configured as `unsafe-none` if multi-threading is not strictly required.
3. If hosting your site on Puter, these headers are handled automatically to allow seamless authentication flow.

title: Missing dangerouslyAllowBrowser flag in OpenAI SDK instantiation under Electron
error_code: OpenAIError: User-supplied API keys in browser
symptoms: Application refuses to compile or compile fails with error

2. Since Puter is keyless and authentication is user-scoped, exposing the token does not present the same risk as exposing your master private OpenAI billable keys.

title: CORS policy blocked request from Capacitor/Cordova on Brave when invoking puter.kv.get()
symptoms: API call fails with Network Error

title: Cross-Origin Opener Policy (COOP) header collision blocks Puter auth popup in MS Edge
symptoms: Auth popup window opens and immediately closes or turns blank
Console error: 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy blocked communication with opener'

These settings isolate the window from any popup window (such as `auth.puter.com`), preventing the parent page from interacting with the authentication frame.
solution:
1. Change your server's COOP header to `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin-allow-popups` instead of `same-origin`. This relaxes isolation specifically to permit popups to communicate back to your opener page.
2. Ensure your `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` is compatible or configured as `unsafe-none` if multi-threading is not strictly required.
3. If hosting your site on Puter, these headers are handled automatically to allow seamless authentication flow.

title: Ad-blockers and privacy settings block guest user frame creation in Brave
symptoms: Puter.js fails to initialize on page load

title: Auth popup fails to return session token to Astro in MS Edge Private Mode
symptoms: Authentication popup opens and signs in successfully, but original window never receives login event
Popup window remains open or closes without logging the user in
Original window reports 'isSignedIn() => false' indefinitely
root_cause: In Private/Incognito tabs or under strict cross-origin policies, browsers block the communication between the popup window (`auth.puter.com`) and the opener window (`window.opener.postMessage`). This blocks Puter's JS SDK from receiving the callback event containing the credentials.
solution:
1. Ensure that the parent page and popup have appropriate communication permissions. Avoid hosting Puter apps inside deeply nested double-iframes.
2. Advise the user to turn off strict cross-site tracking prevention or private browsing tabs if they experience infinite authorization loops.
3. Make sure you don't override the `window.name` or clear `window.opener` inside custom scripts.

title: Puter.js fails to initialize with secure context error on non-local domain
symptoms: Console warning: 'Puter.js requires a secure context (HTTPS) to function correctly.'
Auth and Storage functions throw exceptions or fail silently
Network requests to Puter API fail on non-HTTPS staging sites
root_cause: Puter.js relies heavily on modern Web Cryptography API and service workers for secure token storage and background syncing. Browser security specifications explicitly restrict these APIs to 'Secure Contexts' (HTTPS websites and `http://localhost` or `http://127.0.0.1`). Any deployment to HTTP custom domains or IP addresses will block these APIs, causing Puter.js to fail.
solution:
1. Deploy your web application with SSL enabled. Most providers like Vercel, Netlify, or Puter Hosting provide free automatic SSL certificates.
2. If self-hosting, configure a reverse proxy (like Nginx, Caddy) to terminate SSL and serve your site via HTTPS.
3. For local development on custom subdomains or IP addresses (e.g. `192.168.1.5:3000`), use tools like `mkcert` to generate local SSL certificates, or forward port traffic using SSH tunneling.

title: Localhost IP binding (e.g., http://192.168.x.x) blocking Puter.js on mobile browser testing
symptoms: App works perfectly on desktop `http://localhost:5173`
App fails to run when testing on mobile phone connected to `http://192.168.1.50:5173`
Mobile browser debug log reports that cryptographic APIs are undefined
root_cause: Browsers treat `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` as special safe secure contexts over HTTP. However, when you access your development server via its LAN IP address (`192.168.x.x`), the browser does NOT classify it as a secure context, blocking crucial Web Crypto APIs that Puter.js needs.
solution:
1. Serve the local dev site over HTTPS during LAN mobile tests. Many modern bundlers support this (e.g., `vite --https`).
2. Use a tunnel service like Ngrok, LocalTunnel, or Cloudflare Tunnels to get a free, secure public HTTPS URL pointing to your local server.
3. In Chrome, you can override secure context requirements for testing: Navigate to `chrome://flags/#unsafely-treat-insecure-origin-as-secure`, add `http://192.168.x.x:port` to the list, enable it, and relaunch Chrome.

title: Node.js Serverless Worker sandbox error: undefined globals inside serverless context

root_cause: Puter serverless workers run backend code inside sandboxed execution rums utilizing V8 virtual machine modules (similar to Node's `vm.runInNewContext`). This isolated environment strips dangerous native globals (like direct file system access, process controls, or global network bindings) to secure the host infrastructure. If your script relies on un-sandboxed globals or expects Node core modules, it will crash.
solution:

2. For fetch, ensure the worker environment supports native global fetch (Node 18+). If not, import standard HTTP modules or use `puter.net.fetch()`.
3. Keep workers lightweight and stateless; delegate heavy processing to client-side APIs when safe.
4. Avoid calling dynamic `eval` or writing code that attempts to break out of Node VM isolation.

title: Ad-blockers and privacy settings block guest user frame creation in Chrome
symptoms: Puter.js fails to initialize on page load

title: Auth popup fails to return session token to HTML/JS (CDN) in Firefox Private Mode
symptoms: Authentication popup opens and signs in successfully, but original window never receives login event
Popup window remains open or closes without logging the user in
Original window reports 'isSignedIn() => false' indefinitely
root_cause: In Private/Incognito tabs or under strict cross-origin policies, browsers block the communication between the popup window (`auth.puter.com`) and the opener window (`window.opener.postMessage`). This blocks Puter's JS SDK from receiving the callback event containing the credentials.
solution:

3. Make sure you don't override the `window.name` or clear `window.opener` inside custom scripts.

title: Puter.js fails to initialize with secure context error on non-local domain
symptoms: Console warning: 'Puter.js requires a secure context (HTTPS) to function correctly.'
Auth and Storage functions throw exceptions or fail silently
Network requests to Puter API fail on non-HTTPS staging sites
root_cause: Puter.js relies heavily on modern Web Cryptography API and service workers for secure token storage and background syncing. Any deployment to HTTP custom domains or IP addresses will block these APIs, causing Puter.js to fail.
solution:
1. Deploy your web application with SSL enabled. Most providers like Vercel, Netlify, or Puter Hosting provide free automatic SSL certificates.
2. If self-hosting, configure a reverse proxy (like Nginx, Caddy) to terminate SSL and serve your site via HTTPS.
3. For local development on custom subdomains or IP addresses (e.g. `192.168.1.5:3000`), use tools like `mkcert` to generate local SSL certificates, or forward port traffic using SSH tunneling.

title: Localhost IP binding (e.g., http://192.168.x.x) blocking Puter.js on mobile browser testing
symptoms: App works perfectly on desktop `http://localhost:5173`
App fails to run when testing on mobile phone connected to `http://192.168.1.50:5173`
Mobile browser debug log reports that cryptographic APIs are undefined
root_cause: Browsers treat `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` as special safe secure contexts over HTTP. However, when you access your development server via its LAN IP address (`192.168.x.x`), the browser does NOT classify it as a secure context, blocking crucial Web Crypto APIs that Puter.js needs.
solution:
1. Serve the local dev site over HTTPS during LAN mobile tests. Many modern bundlers support this (e.g., `vite --https`).
2. Use a tunnel service like Ngrok, LocalTunnel, or Cloudflare Tunnels to get a free, secure public HTTPS URL pointing to your local server.
3. In Chrome, you can override secure context requirements for testing: Navigate to `chrome://flags/#unsafely-treat-insecure-origin-as-secure`, add `http://192.168.x.x:port` to the list, enable it, and relaunch Chrome.

title: Node.js Serverless Worker sandbox error: undefined globals inside serverless context
symptoms: Dynamic code evaluation throws: 'ReferenceError: fetch is not defined' or 'window is not defined'
Serverless worker crashes when using standard APIs inside Node VM
Puter workers fail when executing third-party scripts that expect a complete Node/Web environment
root_cause: Puter serverless workers run backend code inside sandboxed execution rums utilizing V8 virtual machine modules (similar to Node's `vm.runInNewContext`). This isolated environment strips dangerous native globals (like direct file system access, process controls, or global network bindings) to secure the host infrastructure. If your script relies on un-sandboxed globals or expects Node core modules, it will crash.
solution:
1. Use Puter's explicit standard libraries provided within the VM context (e.g., use Puter's built-in file APIs instead of native Node `fs`).
2. For fetch, ensure the worker environment supports native global fetch (Node 18+). If not, import standard HTTP modules or use `puter.net.fetch()`.
3. Keep workers lightweight and stateless; delegate heavy processing to client-side APIs when safe.
4. Avoid calling dynamic `eval` or writing code that attempts to break out of Node VM isolation.

title: Serverless Worker execution timeout in sandboxed environment during deepseek/deepseek-r1 tasks
symptoms: Worker returns HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout

root_cause: Puter's serverless VM sandbox imposes strict execution CPU time limits per worker invocation (typically 10-30 seconds depending on plan tier) to prevent server resource starvation. Synchronous blocking code, infinite loops, or attempting to stream massive files synchronously will trigger a timeout kill signal.
solution:
1. Optimize code to run asynchronously and avoid blocking the V8 event loop.
2. For tasks like file parsing or heavy AI formatting, split work into chunks or request operations asynchronously, updating state in the KV store.
3. Make use of client-side streaming when calling models like `deepseek/deepseek-r1`. Stream directly to the browser instead of routing the stream synchronously through a blocking serverless worker.

3. If hosting your site on Puter, these headers are handled automatically to allow seamless authentication flow.

symptoms: Dynamic code evaluation throws: 'ReferenceError: fetch is not defined' or 'window is not defined'
Serverless worker crashes when using standard APIs inside Node VM
Puter workers fail when executing third-party scripts that expect a complete Node/Web environment
root_cause: Puter serverless workers run backend code inside sandboxed execution rums utilizing V8 virtual machine modules (similar to Node's `vm.runInNewContext`). This isolated environment strips dangerous native globals (like direct file system access, process controls, or global network bindings) to secure the host infrastructure. If your script relies on un-sandboxed globals or expects Node core modules, it will crash.
solution:
1. Use Puter's explicit standard libraries provided within the VM context (e.g., use Puter's built-in file APIs instead of native Node `fs`).
2. For fetch, ensure the worker environment supports native global fetch (Node 18+). If not, import standard HTTP modules or use `puter.net.fetch()`.
3. Keep workers lightweight and stateless; delegate heavy processing to client-side APIs when safe.
4. Avoid calling dynamic `eval` or writing code that attempts to break out of Node VM isolation.

title: Serverless Worker execution timeout in sandboxed environment during openai/gpt-5.4-nano tasks
symptoms: Worker returns HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout
Puter.js worker logs report: 'Worker execution exceeded time limits'
Long-running tasks fail mid-way
root_cause: Puter's serverless VM sandbox imposes strict execution CPU time limits per worker invocation (typically 10-30 seconds depending on plan tier) to prevent server resource starvation. Synchronous blocking code, infinite loops, or attempting to stream massive files synchronously will trigger a timeout kill signal.
solution:
1. Optimize code to run asynchronously and avoid blocking the V8 event loop.
2. For tasks like file parsing or heavy AI formatting, split work into chunks or request operations asynchronously, updating state in the KV store.
3. Make use of client-side streaming when calling models like `openai/gpt-5.4-nano`. Stream directly to the browser instead of routing the stream synchronously through a blocking serverless worker.

title: Incorrect base URL configuration in OpenAI SDK when routing to Puter.js in Next.js
symptoms: OpenAI client attempts to query standard OpenAI servers instead of Puter
Authentication errors indicating key is invalid for api.openai.com
HTTP 401 Unauthorized errors returned during ChatCompletion calls
root_cause: To use Puter as a free drop-in replacement for OpenAI SDK, you must override the default `baseURL` parameter in the client configuration to point to Puter's gateway. Failing to do so causes the SDK to call the official OpenAI servers, rejecting your Puter credentials.

title: Model parameter mapping mismatch for 'anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet' in OpenAI SDK configuration
symptoms: API returns 404 Model Not Found or 400 Bad Request
Error message: 'The model "anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet" does not exist or you do not have access to it'
Fallback to standard models fails
